# Fourier Transform on Non-abelian group {#sec-non-abelian}

#### Group function and Group algebra

A group function is a function $f: G \to \mathbb{C}$.
For a finite group $G$ with irreducible representations $\hat G$ and corresponding characters $\chi_{\sigma}: G \to \mathbb{C}$, the Fourier transform of a function $f$ is defined as a mapping from $\hat G$ to $\mathbb{C}^{d_\sigma} \times \mathbb{C}^{d_\sigma}$ satisfying:
$$
\hat{f}(\sigma)=\sqrt{\frac{d_\sigma}{|G|}}\sum_{g \in G} f(g)\sigma(g)
$$
They are all mappings from irreducible representations to $d_{\lambda}$-dimensional unitary matrices.
Similarly, the Fourier transform of a square-integrable function $f: G \to \mathbb{C}$ can be defined as:
$\hat{f}(\lambda)=\int_{g\in G}f(g)\lambda(g)dg,$ where the integral is taken over the invariant measure of the group.

:::{#lem-Fourier-Transform-Properties .callout-important icon="false"}
Fourier Transform on $G$ has the following properties:

1. The Fourier transform of the convolution of two group functions is the product of their transforms
2. The inverse transform satisfies: $f(g) = \sum_{\lambda \in \hat G} d_{\lambda}\text{tr}\left[\lambda(g) \hat f(\lambda)\right]$
3. Parseval's identity: $\int_G dg |f(g)|^2 = \sum_{\lambda \in \hat G}d_{\lambda}\text{tr}\left(\hat f^\dagger(\lambda) \hat f (\lambda)\right)$
:::

The group function $f$ one-to-one corresponds to a group algebra $\mathbb{C}[G]$ element through $f(g) \to \sum_{g \in G} f(g) g$.
The $\mathbb{C}[G]$ have addition and multiplication operations, and works like a matrix algebra, as formalized by the Wedderburn-Artin theorem.

:::{#thm-Wedderburn-Artin .callout-important icon="false"}
## (Wedderburn-Artin theorem)
The finite group algebra $\mathbb{C}[G]$ is isomorphic to the direct sum of the matrix algebras through the map $\text{W-A}: x \to \oplus_{\sigma \in \hat G} \sigma(x)$, where $\sigma(x)$ is the matrix representation of $x$ in the irreducible representation $\sigma$.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Proof
[todo: Add proof]
:::

Under the view of group algebra, we can see that the group function Fourier transform is just the $W-A$ isomorphism.
For $\psi =\sum_{g \in G} f(g) g$, 
$$
\text{W-A}(\psi) =\text{W-A}\left(\sum_{g \in G} f(g) g \right) = \oplus_{\sigma \in \hat G} \sqrt{\frac{d_\sigma}{|G|}}\hat{f}(\sigma).
$$

#### Quantum Fourier Transform

The quantum Fourier transform is the vectorization of the Wedderburn-Artin isomorphism. 
To make this precise, we need two ingredients: a linearization of the group algebra side, and an **isometric** linearization of the matrix algebra side.
For the group algebra side, linearization is straightforward:
$$
\begin{align*}
A = \sum_{g \in G} f(g) g & \xrightarrow{\mathcal{L}}  \ket{A} = \sum_{g \in G} f(g) \ket{g},\\
 g \cdot A &\xrightarrow{\mathcal{L}} L_g \ket{A}, \quad A\cdot g \xrightarrow{\mathcal{L}} R_g\ket{A}.
\end{align*}
$$

For the matrix algebra side, the naive vectorization $E_{jk} \to \ket{j}\ket{k}$ is not the right choice: it fails to be an isometry. The natural inner product on the matrix algebra $\bigoplus_\sigma \mathbb{C}^{d_\sigma \times d_\sigma}$ is the Hilbert-Schmidt inner product $\langle A, B\rangle = \text{tr}(A^\dagger B)$, under which a pure W-A map $x \to \bigoplus_\sigma \sigma(x)$ scales the norm by $|G|$ (unevenly across blocks). To compensate, we define the **isometric vectorization** $\mathcal{L}$ that absorbs the Plancherel measure $d_\sigma / |G|$:
$$
\mathcal{L}(E_{j,k}^\sigma) = \sqrt{\frac{d_\sigma}{|G|}} \ket{\sigma}\ket{j,k}
$$
Under this map, left and right multiplication become:
$$
\begin{align*}
O \cdot M &\to O\otimes \mathbb{I} \,\mathcal{L}(M),\\
M \cdot O &\to \mathbb{I} \otimes O^* \,\mathcal{L}(M).
\end{align*}
$$

:::{#lem-linearization-equivalence .callout-important icon="false"}
## Linearization Equivalence
The quantum Fourier transform
$$
 \mathcal{F}\ket{g} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{|G|}}\sum_{\sigma \in \hat G}d_{\sigma}\ket{\sigma}\otimes \left(\sum_{j,k = 1}^{d_\sigma} \frac{\sigma(g)_{j,k}}{\sqrt{d_{\sigma}} } \ket{j,k}\right)
$$
that operators as a linear transformation on $\ket{g} = \mathcal{L}(g)$ is the linearizaiton $\mathcal{L}$ descripsion of the Wedderburn-Artin isomorphism, i.e., the composition $\mathcal{F} = \mathcal{L} \circ \text{W-A} \circ \mathcal{L}^{-1}$, where $\text{W-A}$ is the **pure, factor-free** algebra homomorphism of @thm-Wedderburn-Artin.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Proof
Explicitly, for a group element $g$:
**Step 1 (pure W-A):**
$$\text{W-A}(g) = \bigoplus_{\sigma \in \hat G} \sigma(g) = \sum_{\sigma \in \hat G}\sum_{j,k=1}^{d_\sigma} \sigma(g)_{j,k}\, E_{j,k}^\sigma$$

**Step 2 (isometric vectorization):**
$$
\begin{align}
\mathcal{L}(\text{W-A}(g)) &= \sum_{\sigma, j, k} \sigma(g)_{j,k} \cdot \sqrt{\frac{d_\sigma}{|G|}}\, \ket{\sigma}\ket{j,k} \nonumber\\
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{|G|}}\sum_{\sigma \in \hat G}d_{\sigma}\ket{\sigma}\otimes \left(\sum_{j,k = 1}^{d_\sigma} \frac{\sigma(g)_{j,k}}{\sqrt{d_{\sigma}} } \ket{j,k}\right) = \mathcal{F}\ket{g}
\end{align}
$$
where $\ket{j,k}$ is the basis of the irreducible representation $\sigma$.
Applying this to the state $\ket{\psi} = \sum_{g \in G} f(g) \ket{g}$ encoding a group algebra element, we verify that the diagram commutes:
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{F}\ket{\psi} &= \sum_{g \in G} f(g)\, \mathcal{L}(\text{W-A}(g))\\
&= \sum_{\sigma \in \hat G} \sum_{j,k=1}^{d_\sigma} \left[ \sqrt{\frac{d_\sigma}{|G|}} \sum_{g \in G} f(g)\,\sigma(g)_{j,k} \right] |\sigma\rangle \otimes |j,k\rangle\\
&= \sum_{\sigma, j, k} \hat{f}(\sigma)_{j,k}\, |\sigma, j, k\rangle = \mathcal{L}\!\left(\text{W-A}\left(\sum_{g \in G} f(g) g \right)\right)
\end{align*}
$$
That is, $\mathcal{F} \circ \mathcal{L}_{\text{group}} = \mathcal{L} \circ \text{W-A}$: the QFT on quantum states is exactly the linearization of the pure Wedderburn-Artin isomorphism.
:::

The multiplication relation in the algebra now becomes the operator equivalence on $\ket{\psi}$ and $\ket{\hat{\psi}}$ by the linearization:
$$
\begin{align*}
L_g \sim \bigoplus_{\sigma \in \hat G} \sigma(g) \otimes \mathbb{I}_{d_\sigma}, \quad R_g \sim \bigoplus_{\sigma \in \hat G} \mathbb{I}_{d_\sigma} \otimes \sigma(g)^*.
\end{align*}
$$

This quivalence is useful since for linear operator on the linearizaiton space, the condition $[A, L_g] = 0, \forall g \in G$ now can be translated to the condition $[\mathcal{F}A\mathcal{F}^\dagger, \bigoplus_{\sigma \in \hat G} \sigma(g) \otimes \mathbb{I}] = 0, \forall g \in G$.
Based on Schur's lemma, this is equivalent to the condition that $\mathcal{F}A\mathcal{F}^\dagger = \mathbb{I} \otimes B$ for some matrix $B$.

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Example: Fourier Transform on $Z_M$ 
Specifically, $Z_M$ with addition modulo $M$ forms an abelian finite group, with one-dimensional irreducible representations labeled by $y \in (0,M-1)$ as $x \to \chi_y(x) = e^{\frac{2 \pi ixy}{M}}=\omega^{xy}$. The Fourier transform on this group is defined as:
$\hat{f}(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{M}}\sum_{y\in\mathbf{Z}_{M}}f(y)\omega^{xy}$
The Fourier transform on this group is defined as:
$$
\begin{align*}
\ket{x} \to \ket{\hat x}= \frac{1}{\sqrt{M}}\sum_{y = 0}^{M -1}e^{\frac{2 \pi ixy}{M}}\ket{y}
\end{align*}
$$
It is the same as the classical FT expression, but note that the input is not $2^n$ complex numbers, but the change of probability distribution.
This transformation can be implemented with a shallow circuit [1].

:::

# Symmetric of Hidden Subgroup Finding

#### Application to Hidden Subgroup Problem

As reviewed in Shor algortihms, a typical HSP algorithms runs like below:

:::{.callout-note icon="false"}
## Algorithm: Hidden Subgroup Finding
**Input:** Given an group $G$ and a group function $f : G \to S$, S not necessarily be $\mathbb{C}$.

**Output:** The generators of the subgroup $H:= \{h \in G| \forall g \in G, f(g) = f(hg)\}$.

1. Combine classical reversible circuit design, prepare the state $\frac{1}{\sqrt{|G|}}\sum_g\ket{g}\ket{f(g)}$, and measure the latter to get $\ket{\psi} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{|H|}} \sum_{h \in H} \ket{c h} := \ket{c H}$ if the measurement result if $f(c)$ for the second register.
2. Implement quantum Fourier transform on the group $G$ to get $\ket{\tilde{\psi}} = \mathcal{F}_G \ket{\psi}$.
3. implement certain POVMs on $\ket{\tilde{\psi}}$ to get the generators.
:::

:::{.callout-important collapse="true"}
## Note
The sufficiency of the computational basis measurement in the Abelian case is guaranteed by three facts:

1. **Absence of internal matrix degrees of freedom:** For an abelian group, all irreducible representations are one-dimensional ($d_\sigma = 1$). The complicated output space $|\sigma\rangle \otimes |j,k\rangle$ collapses simply to $|\sigma\rangle$, which corresponds precisely to the computational basis $|y\rangle$ of the dual group. The problem of "basis selection" (which necessitates POVMs in non-abelian cases) natively vanishes.
2. **Phase erasure of the coset shift:** The QFT maps the random coset representative $g_0$ into a global phase $\chi_y(g_0) = e^{\frac{2\pi i g_0 y}{|G|}}$ attached to each basis state $|y\rangle$. Measuring in the computational basis takes the modulus squared, cleanly wiping out this random shift information and yielding a probability distribution that depends strictly on the orthogonal subgroup $H^\perp$.
3. **Classical tractability:** The standard measurement yields elements uniformly distributed over $H^\perp$ (or concentrated around the interference peaks in Shor's approximate case). Mathematically, an $O(\log |G|)$ number of such classical samples is theoretically complete to generate the entire $H^\perp$, allowing us to efficiently reconstruct the hidden subgroup $H = (H^\perp)^\perp$ using classical linear algebra or continued fraction algorithms.
:::

The step 2 and 3 are well designed in the abelian case, as reviewed through [Shor's algorithm](/knowledge/Factoring/shor.html), where measuring the state $\ket{\tilde{\psi}}$ directly in the standard computational basis is perfectly sufficient.
But in the non-abelian case, we must carefully design specific POVMs (or entangled multi-register measurements) to extract information. 

:::{#lem-lowerbd_HSP .callout-important icon="false"}
## Lower Bound for HSP
Given a group function $f$ such $f(c)$ will not give us any information about the left-coset index $c$. 
Ensure that $f$ has hidden subgroup: (i). $g^{-1}Hg$ for some $g \in G$ and some known $H$ or (ii). the trivial subgroup $\{e\}$.
Then any algorithms $\mathcal{A}$ that distinguish (i) and (ii), there exists a $\sigma \in \hat{G}$ and a vector $b_k \in \mathbb{C}^{d_\sigma}$,such that the distribution set
$$
\{P_{g}(k|\sigma)\}_{g \in G}, \quad P_{g}(k|\sigma) = a_k  \frac{\|\sigma(\Pi_H) \sigma(g) b_k^*\|^2}{\mathrm{tr}(\sigma(\Pi_H))},
$$
is indistinguishable from average distribution under $\mathcal{A}$ with the same complexity.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Proof

The output state is actually a mixed state, with the density matrix:
$$
\rho = |G|^{-1}\sum_{c \in G} \ket{c H}\!\bra{c H}
$$
This quantum state is invariant under left-multiplication $L_g \ket{h} = \ket{gh}$, thus any POVM $\{\mu_j\}_{j=1}^m$ can be symmetrized to $\mu'_j = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G} L_g^\dagger \mu_j L_g$ such that $[\mu'_j, L_g] = 0$ for all $g \in G$.
This means that $\mathcal{F}\mu'_j \mathcal{F}^\dagger = \bigoplus_{\sigma \in \hat G} \lambda_{\sigma} \cdot \mathbb{I}_{d_\sigma} \otimes B_{\sigma, j}$ for all $j$.

To maximize the information extracted, we can strictly refine this POVM.
This mathematically decouples the measurement into a two-step physical process:

- **Weak Fourier Sampling:** Projector $\Pi(\sigma) := \mathbb{I}_{d_\sigma} \otimes \mathbb{I}_{d_\sigma}$ with result $\sigma$.
- **Strong Fourier Sampling:** Conditionally on known $\sigma$, a rank-1 POVM $\{a_k \mathbb{I}_{d_\sigma} \otimes |b_{\sigma, k}\rangle \!\langle b_{\sigma, k}|\}_{k}$ with result $k$ such that $|b_{\sigma, k}\rangle$ is $d_\sigma$-dimensional state.

Apply Fourier transformation on state $\ket{H}$ gives:
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{F}\ket{H} &=\sum_{h \in H} \sqrt{\frac{d_{\sigma}}{|G||H|}} \sum_{\sigma \in \hat G}  \ket{\sigma} \otimes \left(\sum_{j,k = 1}^{d_\sigma} \sigma(h)_{j,k} \ket{j,k}\right)
\end{align*}
$$
Implementing the weak Fourier sampling $\{\mathbb{I}_{d_\sigma} \otimes \mathbb{I}_{d_\sigma}\}_{\sigma \in \hat G}$, we get the post-measurement state:
$$
\begin{align*}
\left(\mathbb{I}_{d_\sigma} \otimes \mathbb{I}_{d_\sigma}\right) \mathcal{F}\ket{H} &= \sum_{h \in H} \sqrt{\frac{d_{\sigma}}{|G||H|}} \ket{\sigma} \otimes \left(\sum_{j,k = 1}^{d_\sigma} \sigma(h)_{j,k} \ket{j,k}\right)\\
&=\sqrt{\frac{d_{\sigma}|H|}{|G|}} \ket{\sigma} \otimes \left( \sum_{j,k = 1}^{d_\sigma} \sigma\left(|H|^{-1}\sum_{h \in H} h\right)_{j,k} \ket{j,k}\right) \\
&=\sqrt{\frac{d_{\sigma}|H|}{|G|}} \ket{\sigma} \otimes  \ket{\sigma(\Pi_H)},
\end{align*}
$$
where $\Pi_H := |H|^{-1}\sum_{h \in H} h$ and $\ket{\sigma(\Pi_H)}$ is vectorization of $\sigma(\Pi_H)$.
the result $\sigma$ appear with probability:
$$
\begin{align*}
P(\sigma) &= \frac{d_{\sigma}|H|}{|G|} \left\|\ket{\sigma(\Pi_H)}\right\|^2
&= \frac{d_{\sigma}}{|G||H|} \mathrm{tr}(\sigma(\Pi_H \cdot \Pi_H^\dagger)) \\
&= \frac{d_{\sigma}|H|}{|G|} \mathrm{tr}\left(\sigma(\Pi_H)\right).
\end{align*}
$$
Here in the last line, we use the fact $H$ is a subgroup of $G$ thus $\Pi_H = \Pi_H^\dagger= \Pi_H^2$.
Implementing the strong Fourier sampling with result $k$ gives post-measurement state (if we suppose $\sqrt{a_k}\ket{b_k}\!\bra{b_k}$ as the measurement Kraus operator):
$$
\begin{align*}
\ket{\psi_{\text{post}}} & = \sqrt{a_k}\sqrt{\frac{d_{\sigma}|H|}{|G|}} \ket{\sigma} \otimes (\mathbb{I}_{d_\sigma} \otimes |b_k\rangle\langle b_k|) \ket{\sigma(\Pi_H)} \\
&= \sqrt{a_k}\sqrt{\frac{d_{\sigma}|H|}{|G|}} \ket{\sigma} \otimes \Big( \sigma(\Pi_H)\ket{b_k^*} \Big) \otimes \ket{b_k},
\end{align*}
$$
where we use the fact  $(\mathbb{I} \otimes \ket{v}\!\bra{v} ) \cdot \ket{B} = B \ket{v^*} \otimes \ket{v}$.
The result $k$ appear with probability:
$$
\begin{align*}
P(\sigma, k) &= \left\| \ket{\psi_{\text{post}}} \right\|^2 = a_k \frac{d_{\sigma}|H|}{|G|} \Big\| \sigma(\Pi_H)\ket{b_k^*} \Big\|^2 \\
&=a_k \frac{d_{\sigma}|H|}{|G|} \bra{b_k^*} \sigma(\Pi_H) \ket{b_k^*}.
\end{align*}
$$

We note that the subgroup $H$ and the conjugated subgroup $g^{-1} H g$ have the same weak Fourier sampling distribution $P(\rho)$ for any $g \in G$. The strong Fourier sampling distribution reflects $g$ throught the conditional probability
$$
P_{g}(k|\sigma) = a_k \bra{b_k^*} \frac{\sigma(g^{-1}\Pi_H g)}{\mathrm{tr}(\sigma(\Pi_H))} \ket{b_k^*} = a_k  \frac{\|\sigma(\Pi_H) \sigma(g) b_k^*\|^2}{\mathrm{tr}(\sigma(\Pi_H))}.
$$
Thus, to prove the ineffectiveness of the Fourier sampling on the tasks of giving the generators of $H$, it is sufficient to show the hardness in distinguishing from distribution $\{P_{g}(k|\sigma)\}_{g \in G}$.
:::
